title: Jupiter and Lycaon: Judgment and Change
subtitle: A test of divine power in Ovid's Book I

lycaon.author: Ovid
lycaon.locator: Book I · Fable VII [I.216-243]; Book I · Fable VII [I.216-243], normalized characters 361-1445
lycaon.excerpt: In the first place, Lycaon derided their pious supplications. Afterwards, he said, I will make trial, by a plain proof, whether this is a God, or whether he is a mortal; nor shall the truth remain a matter of doubt. He then makes preparations to destroy me, when sunk in sleep, by an unexpected death; this mode of testing the truth pleases him. And not content with that, with the sword he cuts the throat of an hostage that had been sent from the nation of the Molossians,[45] and then softens part of the quivering limbs, in boiling water, and part he roasts with fire placed beneath. Soon as he had placed these on the table, I, with avenging flames, overthrew the house upon the household Gods,[46] worthy of their master. Alarmed, he himself takes to flight, and having reached the solitude of the country, he howls aloud, and in vain attempts to speak; his mouth gathers rage from himself, and through its {usual} desire for slaughter, it is directed against the sheep, and even still delights in blood. His garments are changed into hair, his arms into legs; he becomes a wolf

narrativeBlocks.title: The council of the gods
narrativeBlocks.body: Jupiter summons the gods to report on humanity: the wickedness has grown unbearable, and he tells them of the test he ran in person on King Lycaon of Arcadia.

narrativeBlocks.title: The feast of human flesh
narrativeBlocks.body: Disguised as a mortal, Jupiter visits Lycaon's court. The king, to see whether his guest is truly a god, murders a hostage and serves the flesh at dinner — a crime dressed as an experiment.

narrativeBlocks.title: The lightning answer
narrativeBlocks.body: Jupiter's lightning blasts the palace; Lycaon flees howling into the fields — and the howl continues as his body changes: his savagery made literal, he becomes a wolf.

narrativeBlocks.title: The case for the flood
narrativeBlocks.body: One monster convicted, Jupiter argues the whole species has failed — and the gods agree: the flood that will drown the world is coming. Lycaon is the evidence.

narrativeBlocks.title: Ovid's Roman frame
narrativeBlocks.body: This flood is not Mesopotamia's whim or the Bible's covenant — in Ovid it is a judgment on a corrupt age, argued before a senate of gods, with the wolf-king as Exhibit A.
